catalog_quote: Primary stress is almost invariably found on the penultimate syllable. In words of four syllables or more, a secondary stress attaches to the preceding syllable but one. ... Thus: ['nvat] 'stone' ['movoy] 'outrigger pole' [na'lintoy] 'lobster' [sesi'maqsi] 'index finger' It should be noted that stress assignment occurs after all morphophonemic processes have applied. This means that stress does not necessarily attach to root syllables only, as affixed syllables can also be stressed. Syllabic material that is inserted or deleted morphophonemically within roots is also counted in the normal way for stress assignment purposes. new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the surface word (monosyllables stressed on their only vowel); stress is computed on the output of all morphophonemic processes, so suffixes and inserted/deleted syllables count and affixal syllables can bear stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Crowley 2002: in words of four or more syllables, secondary stress on the syllable two before the primary (i.e. alternating leftward, e.g. [ˌsesi'maŋsi]). Lynch & Capell 1983 p. 22 instead place secondary stress on the initial syllable of words of more than three syllables (['orutenmoŋi]); Lynch 2001 p. 9: 'normally two syllables to the left of the primary-stressed syllable'.
new_statements.exceptions: Crowley: 'almost invariably' penultimate (no list given in the sketch). Lynch & Capell 1983 pp. 21-22: 'a handful of words with stress on the final syllable' (Capell's MS recorded some irregularly final-stressed nouns such as breadfruit [nmar] < nemar, which Lynch links to pretonic vowel loss); epenthetic schwa/copy vowels breaking heterorganic consonant clusters are never stressed and are not counted as syllables for stress assignment ([nov(ə)'laimp(ə)ɣon] 'its tail').
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule stated over inflected surface words including affixes (Crowley's examples are affixed verb forms [ɣ-o'roŋ-yau] '(s)he heard me', ['ɣ-orŋ-oŋ], [ɣo'ɣ-orŋ-i]); examples are citation forms; no phrase-level discussion. No vowel-length contrast in Sye (unlike Tanna/Anejom where long final vowels attract stress).
new_statements.identity_note: All three modern sources describe the same language under two spellings: Sie (Lynch & Capell 1983) and Sye (Crowley 1998/2000/2002), glottocode siee1239, ISO erg, the modern language of Erromango. Crowley 2002 is an abridgment of Crowley 1998, based largely on speaker Edward Nalial. Lynch 2001's 'Erromango' generalisation covers Sye and moribund Ura (urav1235) together.

new_statements.quote: 1.5. Stress. Apart from a handful of words with stress on the final syllable, primary stress in Sie falls on the vowel of a monosyllable and the penultimate vowel of a polysyllable: (23) /nup/ ... yam; /nomu/ ... fish; /umole/ ... ant. Epenthetic vowels inserted to break up heterorganic consonant clusters are not stressed, nor are they counted as syllabic in the assignment of stress: (24) /nelve-n/ ... his tooth; /novlaimpgo-n/ ... its tail; /mehkai/ ... six. Secondary stress occurs on the initial syllable of words of more than three syllables: (25) /orutenmoŋi/ ... to sink (trans.); /osavlahakŋi/ ... to turn over (trans.) [p. 21, sec. 1.4:] Capell's MS also notes that a number of these forms were (irregularly) stressed on the final syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog (penultimate) and as Crowley 2002; adds that epenthetic vowels are invisible to stress, that a handful of words (Capell's initial-CC forms) carry final stress, and a secondary-stress rule (initial syllable of 4+-syllable words). Crowley 2002 puts the secondary stress on 'the preceding syllable but one' (two syllables before the primary), which coincides with Lynch & Capell's initial-syllable rule only in four-syllable words; for five-syllable-plus words the two statements differ slightly. Ch. 1 (pp. 1-9) and ch. 7 (Proto-Erromangan) contain nothing synchronic on stress (ch. 7 only notes that unstressed non-final vowels were often lost historically). Ch. 4 (Ura,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate vowel of polysyllables (and on the single vowel of monosyllables); epenthetic vowels breaking heterorganic clusters are not syllables for stress assignment; secondary stress on the initial syllable of words of more than three syllables. (Word-count spacing in the quote normalised from the scanned text; the bracketed phonetic forms after each example are omitted because the scanned garbles the stress marks.)
new_statements.secondary_stress: Initial syllable of words of more than three syllables (ex. 25: /orutenmoŋi/ 'to sink (trans.)', /osavlahakŋi/ 'to turn over (trans.)').
new_statements.exceptions: 'a handful of words with stress on the final syllable'; Capell's MS records that a number of initial-CC forms (devat 'four', nevat 'stone', nemar 'breadfruit', etc.) were '(irregularly) stressed on the final syllable', which Lynch takes as the cause of pretonic /e/ loss; epenthetic vowels are never stressed and do not count for stress; all vowels may reduce to schwa in a pretonic syllable (p. 16).
new_statements.identity_note: Ch. 2 of the volume describes the Dillon's Bay (central west coast) dialect of Sie, which Lynch & Capell say 'forms the basis for the present study'; Ifo and Potnarvin lists show virtually no structural variation (p. 11). Sie is described as the continuation of Yoku, affected by extinct Sorung. Ch. 4 of the same volume concerns Ura (uraa1240), a separate Erromangan language, for which it says only that stress tends to be penultimate.

sources.citation: Lynch, John. 2001. The linguistic history of Southern Vanuatu. Pacific Linguistics 509. Canberra: ANU. [sec. 1.5.2 p. 9; ch. 4 Proto Southern Vanuatu stress pp. 101-117]
sources.note: p. 9: 'Primary stress is invariably on the penultimate syllable in Erromango. In Anejom and the Tanna languages, it is normally penultimate, but (a) final if the vowel of the final syllable is long, and (b) antepenultimate in certain very restricted contexts. Secondary stress normally occurs two syllables to the left of the primary-stressed syllable.' Ch. 4 reconstructs PSV stress (penultimate if final syllable open, final if closed) - historical.
